title: Load shedding and graceful degradation
subtitle: When more work arrives than you can finish, drop the least important part early and cheaply, so the important part still works.

c.v: In 2019, Netflix had an outage. A sizable share of members could not play for a period of time.
Netflix lists many things that can overload its systems. A client bug can trigger a
. A backend can be under-scaled. A deploy can be bad, or the network or cloud provider can have problems. Each of these had stopped members from playing at some point.
At the time, Netflix had on/off
. It had "no progressive way to shed load".
So the team built one into Zuul, its
. Each request gets a priority. When things go wrong, low-priority requests are dropped first.

In 2020, days after the change went live, a similar problem hit. It had the same potential impact as the 2019 outage. This time Zuul shed traffic until the service was healthy again, "without impacting members' ability to play at all".
The problem was just as serious. The difference was that the system chose what to drop.
Every server has a limit. When more work arrives than it can finish, some work will fail. You cannot avoid that. You can only choose which work fails, and how.
Without a plan, the server tries to do everything. Then nearly everything fails. With
, the server rejects some requests early and finishes the rest in time.

goes one step further. It cuts the work per request, for example by serving a slightly stale local copy of the data.
Overload means some work will fail. Decide in advance which work that is. Drop it early, cheaply and on purpose, so the important work still finishes in time.

The trap is that the server looks busy and healthy. It finishes as many requests as ever. But the client has already timed out, so the work is wasted. Amazon calls the useful part

A rejection must cost much less than real work. Amazon says early rejection "is the cheapest place to drop excess traffic".

Google warns that rejecting is not always cheap. For a simple memory lookup, rejecting costs almost as much as serving.
Shedding has limits, so you still need capacity.
A simple server-side signal is the number of requests in flight. Over a limit, return HTTP 503 to new requests.
Google also uses CPU and rejects by criticality as use nears a threshold.
Not all requests are equal. Netflix sorts its traffic into three classes:
: logs and background requests. They do not affect playback, but they are a large share of load.
: features like viewing history and pause markers. Users notice, but can still play.

Zuul gives each request a score from 1 to 100 as its first step.

Under overload it drops requests below a moving threshold. A cubic curve moves the threshold slowly at first, then sharply. At 35% overload the threshold is still in the mid-90s. At 80% it reaches 50.

Queue order: controlled delay and adaptive LIFO
Facebook found that "many of our worst incidents" had large numbers of requests waiting in queues.
In 2015, Facebook described using two ideas together.
, a variant of the CoDel algorithm from network research. If the queue has not been empty in the last 100 ms, a new request may wait only 5 ms. Otherwise it may wait up to 100 ms.
Short bursts still queue, but a standing queue cannot form. Facebook found these values work well for most services, without tuning for each one.
In a long queue, the oldest request's user may have already left. So the server uses
normally, then switches to LIFO when a queue starts to form.
The newest requests then have the best chance to finish in time.

Shedding drops whole requests. Degradation does less work per request. Google's examples: search a smaller in-memory set instead of the disk, or use a cheaper ranking.

c.v: "At twice our peak, what fails first? Did we choose that?"
Write down the priority class of each endpoint with the product owner. Payment is not the same as a recommendations widget.
Watch goodput, not only throughput. Count requests that finished in time and without error, and tie it to your
Count shed requests by class and alert when critical traffic is shed.
Load test past the breaking point before big events. Check that goodput levels off.
Review client retry rules. They should honor
and stop when most calls fail.
"Add an admission check to this service. Count requests in flight. Read a priority from the
header (critical, degraded, sheddable). Reject over a per-class limit with 503 and Retry-After, before parsing the body."
"Propagate the client deadline through every call in this handler. Before each downstream call, drop the request if less than 50 ms is left."
"Write a load test that ramps from 50% to 300% of measured capacity. Plot throughput, goodput and p99 latency per priority class."
The rejection happens before any expensive work: no body parsing, database call or downstream call.

Every endpoint has a priority, and unknown traffic gets a low class, not critical.

q.v: A server can finish 1,000 requests a second. 1,500 a second arrive, and it queues the extra in FIFO order with no limit. Clients give up after 1 second. What happens after a few seconds?

options.v: The server finishes 1,000 a second, and nearly all of them reach a client that is still waiting.
The server finishes about 1,000 a second, but almost every answer comes after its caller gave up.
The server finishes fewer requests, but each one is fast.

why.v: The queue grows by 500 a second, so the wait soon passes 1 second. The server stays busy, but goodput falls close to zero.

q.v: What is the main difference between a rate limit and load shedding?

options.v: A rate limit is usually per client and fixed ahead of time. Load shedding reacts to the server's own state, such as CPU or requests in flight.
A rate limit returns 503, and load shedding returns 429.
Load shedding only runs on the client.

why.v: A rate limit stops one client using more than its share. Load shedding protects the server when total load is too high, whoever sends it.

q.v: In Netflix's taxonomy, which traffic is shed first?

options.v: CRITICAL, such as the request to start playback.
NON_CRITICAL, such as logs and background requests.

why.v: Shedding starts with the lowest priority. Logs and background requests do not affect playback, and they are a large share of the load.

q.v: Under Facebook's adaptive LIFO, when does the server switch from FIFO to LIFO?

options.v: Always. LIFO is faster in general.
When a queue starts to form, because the oldest requests are the most likely to be abandoned.
Only for requests marked as critical.

why.v: In normal times the queue is short and FIFO is fair. Under queuing, the newest request is the one most likely to still have a waiting user.

q.v: With Google's adaptive throttling (K = 2), a client made 100 requests in the last 2 minutes and the backend accepted 30. About what share of new requests does the client reject locally?

options.v: 0%, because the backend still accepts some requests.

why.v: The rejection chance is max(0, (requests − K × accepts) / (requests + 1)). That is 40 / 101, about 40%.
